# Design

How this app is built: its stack, layout and conventions.
Read it with `AGENTS.md`, which has the working rules and how the app is tested.

*TanStack's own documentation is vendored in this repo under `docs/tanstack/`: the official
`llms.txt` index for TanStack Router (`router.llms.txt`) and TanStack Query (`query.llms.txt`).
Consult it when working with TanStack Router or Query.*

---

## OfficeFloor REST endpoints — routes MUST live under `rest/api/`

Put every domain REST route under `src/main/resources/officefloor/rest/api/` so its path starts
with `/api/`: `SpaConfig` only lets `/api/*` reach the backend, and a non-`/api/` route is swallowed
by the SPA deep-link fallback (it returns `index.html`, not your endpoint). The reference below uses
non-`/api/` example paths for brevity — in this app the `/api/` prefix is required. See
`src/main/resources/officefloor/README.md`.

---

*The following is OfficeFloor's own agent guidance for this stack, included verbatim
from <https://officefloor.net/AGENTS.md>. It is part of the OfficeFloor architecture.*

## OfficeFloor REST endpoints

Applies when adding or changing REST endpoints. This project serves REST through
OfficeFloor Function Injection, **not** Spring MVC controllers: each endpoint is a
pipeline of small function classes wired together in YAML.

- Requires the OfficeFloor Spring Boot starter in the build:
  `officefloor-rest-spring-boot-4-starter` (Spring Boot 4.x) or
  `officefloor-rest-spring-boot-3-starter` (Spring Boot 3.x). Without it these YAML
  files are inert. (Rules below track these starter versions.)
- Define each endpoint as a YAML file under `src/main/resources/officefloor/rest/`,
  named `<path>.<METHOD>.yml` (e.g. `owners/{ownerId}.PUT.yml` → `PUT /owners/{ownerId}`).
- One small function class per step; compose steps with `next:` and `outputs:`.
- Do NOT generate `@RestController`, `@GetMapping` or `@PostMapping`.
- Transactions: `govern: [ transaction ]` on steps, not `@Transactional`.
- Errors: a handler YAML in `officefloor/escalation/`, not `@ControllerAdvice`.

### Worked example — `PUT /owners/{ownerId}`

The whole shape of an endpoint. The sections after this one are the reference.

`src/main/resources/officefloor/rest/owners/{ownerId}.PUT.yml`

```yaml
# First step runs first. Validate before Load so an invalid body is a 400,
# not masked by a 404 for a missing owner.
validate:
  class: com.example.owner.ValidateOwner
  next: load
load:
  class: com.example.owner.LoadOwner
  next: apply
apply:
  class: com.example.owner.ApplyOwner
  govern: [ transaction ]
  next: save
save:
  class: com.example.owner.SaveOwner
  govern: [ transaction ]
  next: respond
respond:
  class: com.example.owner.RespondWithOwner
```

```java
// One public method each. State moves by Out<T> (set) → @Val (read), matched by type.
public class ValidateOwner {
  public void validate(@RequestBody @Valid OwnerRequest request, Out<OwnerRequest> body) {
    body.set(request); // body read once here; republished for later steps
  }
}
public class LoadOwner {
  public void load(@PathVariable("ownerId") int ownerId, OwnerRepository repository,
      Out<Owner> ownerOut) throws OwnerNotFoundException {
    Owner owner = repository.findById(ownerId);
    if (owner == null) throw new OwnerNotFoundException(ownerId); // handled below
    ownerOut.set(owner);
  }
}
public class ApplyOwner { // @Val yields the stored object, not a copy — mutate in place
  public void apply(@Val OwnerRequest request, @Val Owner owner) {
    owner.setFirstName(request.firstName());
    owner.setLastName(request.lastName());
  }
}
public class SaveOwner {
  public void save(@Val Owner owner, OwnerRepository repository) {
    repository.save(owner);
  }
}
public class RespondWithOwner {
  public void respond(@Val Owner owner, ObjectResponse<OwnerResponse> response) {
    response.send(OwnerResponse.from(owner)); // this step responds; 200 by default
  }
}
```

`src/main/resources/officefloor/escalation/com.example.owner.OwnerNotFoundException.yml`

```yaml
handle:
  class: com.example.owner.HandleOwnerNotFound
```

```java
public class HandleOwnerNotFound {
  public void handle(@Parameter OwnerNotFoundException ex,
      ObjectResponse<ResponseEntity<String>> response) {
    response.send(new ResponseEntity<>(ex.getMessage(), HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND));
  }
}
```

### Step wiring

Each top-level YAML entry is a developer-chosen step name; the first is the entry
point. `class:` names the function. **Give each function class exactly one public
method** — several public methods fail at start-up unless every reference adds
`method:`.

- `next: <step>` — run that step afterwards. This step's return value arrives there
  as `@Parameter T`.
- `outputs: { <name>: <step> }` — conditional branches. Declare a
  `@FunctionalInterface` parameter annotated `@Flow("<name>")` and call it to take the
  branch; not calling it short-circuits.

### Function parameters

Declare only what the step needs; they resolve by role:

- `@PathVariable`, `@RequestParam`, `@RequestBody` — Spring MVC annotations work.
- Spring beans (repositories, mappers, services) — injected by type as normal.
- `ObjectResponse<T>` (`net.officefloor.web.ObjectResponse`) — send the response with
  `response.send(dto)`. This is how a step responds; wrap as
  `ObjectResponse<ResponseEntity<T>>` to set status explicitly.
- `@Parameter T` (`net.officefloor.plugin.section.clazz.Parameter`) — the previous
  step's return value, a `@Flow` argument, or a thrown escalation.

### Passing state between steps — `Out<T>` / `@Val`

Steps do not call each other. Beyond the single `@Parameter` hand-off, publish state
into a variable (`net.officefloor.plugin.variable`):

- Producer declares `Out<T>` and calls `set(...)`; consumer declares `@Val T`.
- Matching is **by type** — two variables of the same type in one pipeline need a
  `@Qualifier` annotation to disambiguate.
- `@Val` yields the same object the producer stored, **not a copy** — so an `Apply`
  step mutates the entity in place and later steps see the change.

### Naming

Verb plus entity: `Load<E>` (fetch by path variable, publishes `Out<E>`, throws when
absent) · `Build<E>` (construct from body) · `Validate<E>` (bind and validate the body,
publish it) · `Apply<E>` (mutate) · `Save<E>` · `Delete<E>` · `RespondWith<E>` (200) ·
`RespondWith<E>Created` (201) · `RespondWithNoContent` (204).

Keep DTOs at the edges — request body in at the first step, response DTO out at the
responder. Steps in between work with entities.

### Request body and validation

- The HTTP body can be read only once: **only one step per pipeline may bind
  `@RequestBody`**. A second binding fails at runtime. When later steps need it, the
  first step publishes it as a variable.
- `@Valid` runs before that step's method body, so step order decides when validation
  happens. Put the validating step first — otherwise a missing id returns 404 before an
  invalid body can return 400.

### Transactions

`govern: [ transaction ]` for writes, `govern: [ readonly-transaction ]` for reads,
listed on **every** step it covers. Both are provided by the starter. Governance spans
the pipeline, so the request commits once at the end.

### Errors

Functions throw; handlers respond. The exception must be **checked** (`extends
Exception`) so it appears in the `throws` clause. Put the handler in
`officefloor/escalation/<fully.qualified.ExceptionClass>.yml`, taking the exception as
`@Parameter` and responding via `ObjectResponse`. Matching is most-specific-first;
anything unmatched falls through to Spring `@RestControllerAdvice`.

### Security

Guard a whole endpoint file with a Spring Security SpEL expression:

```yaml
composition:
  authorize: "hasRole('OWNER_ADMIN')"
```

-- A sheet's terms per grade: the days after a claim's date that a claim of that grade is due by.
-- A grade with no row uses the sheet's terms.
CREATE TABLE grade_terms (
    sheet_id VARCHAR(200) NOT NULL REFERENCES sheet(id),
    grade CHAR(1) NOT NULL,
    terms INT NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (sheet_id, grade)
);
-- A claim's due-by, fixed when it is made: its date plus the terms of its person's grade in force on
-- its date. It does not move when the terms or the claim's date change later.
ALTER TABLE claim ADD COLUMN due_by DATE;
UPDATE claim SET due_by = DATEADD('DAY', (SELECT s.terms FROM sheet s WHERE s.id = claim.sheet_id), claim_date);
ALTER TABLE claim ALTER COLUMN due_by SET NOT NULL;
-- A person's own terms, in days: when set, a claim of theirs is due-by its date plus these, ahead of
-- their grade's terms and the sheet's. NULL: they have none.
ALTER TABLE person ADD COLUMN terms INT;
-- The history a statement taken as of a date reads: every change below is kept with the sheet's
-- today when it was made (set_on / made_on / added_on), so the figures as they stood at the end of a
-- date are those of the changes made while the sheet's today was on or before it. What was already
-- stored before this history was kept counts from the beginning of time (0001-01-01, or null).

-- The sheet's today when the person was added (null: from the beginning of time).
ALTER TABLE person ADD COLUMN added_on DATE;

-- Every rate set, oldest first: the rate in force for a grade and from-date as of a date is the
-- last one set for them on or before it.
CREATE TABLE rate_history (
    id BIGINT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
    sheet_id VARCHAR(200) NOT NULL REFERENCES sheet(id),
    grade CHAR(1) NOT NULL,
    pct DECIMAL(19, 2) NOT NULL,
    from_date DATE,
    to_date DATE,
    set_on DATE NOT NULL
);
CREATE INDEX rate_history_sheet ON rate_history(sheet_id, id);
INSERT INTO rate_history (sheet_id, grade, pct, from_date, to_date, set_on)
    SELECT sheet_id, grade, pct, from_date, to_date, DATE '0001-01-01' FROM rate;

-- Every dated setting value recorded, oldest first, and every policy date set (key policy-date,
-- no from-date, '' for none).
CREATE TABLE setting_history (
    id BIGINT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
    sheet_id VARCHAR(200) NOT NULL REFERENCES sheet(id),
    setting_key VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL,
    from_date DATE,
    setting_value VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL,
    set_on DATE NOT NULL
);
CREATE INDEX setting_history_sheet ON setting_history(sheet_id, id);
INSERT INTO setting_history (sheet_id, setting_key, from_date, setting_value, set_on)
    SELECT sheet_id, setting_key, from_date, setting_value, DATE '0001-01-01' FROM setting_value;
INSERT INTO setting_history (sheet_id, setting_key, from_date, setting_value, set_on)
    SELECT id, 'policy-date', NULL, CAST(policy_date AS VARCHAR), DATE '0001-01-01' FROM sheet WHERE policy_date IS NOT NULL;

-- Every grade a person was given, oldest first: the first grade (no from-date) or a dated one.
CREATE TABLE person_grade_history (
    id BIGINT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
    sheet_id VARCHAR(200) NOT NULL REFERENCES sheet(id),
    person_id BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES person(id),
    from_date DATE,
    grade CHAR(1) NOT NULL,
    set_on DATE NOT NULL
);
CREATE INDEX person_grade_history_sheet ON person_grade_history(sheet_id, person_id, id);
INSERT INTO person_grade_history (sheet_id, person_id, from_date, grade, set_on)
    SELECT sheet_id, id, NULL, grade, DATE '0001-01-01' FROM person;
INSERT INTO person_grade_history (sheet_id, person_id, from_date, grade, set_on)
    SELECT sheet_id, person_id, from_date, grade, DATE '0001-01-01' FROM person_grade;

-- Every retirement date a person was given, oldest first.
CREATE TABLE person_retirement (
    id BIGINT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
    sheet_id VARCHAR(200) NOT NULL REFERENCES sheet(id),
    person_id BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES person(id),
    from_date DATE,
    set_on DATE NOT NULL
);
CREATE INDEX person_retirement_sheet ON person_retirement(sheet_id, person_id, id);
INSERT INTO person_retirement (sheet_id, person_id, from_date, set_on)
    SELECT sheet_id, id, retired_from, DATE '0001-01-01' FROM person WHERE retired_from IS NOT NULL;

-- The sheet's today when a hold was added (null: from the beginning of time).
ALTER TABLE person_hold ADD COLUMN made_on DATE;

-- Every change to a claim's statement binding, oldest first: bound (with its figure, null: n/a) or
-- left unbound. A claim with no line on or before a date was unbound then.
CREATE TABLE claim_binding (
    id BIGINT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
    sheet_id VARCHAR(200) NOT NULL REFERENCES sheet(id),
    claim_id BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES claim(id),
    stated BOOLEAN NOT NULL,
    stated_due DECIMAL(19, 2),
    set_on DATE NOT NULL
);
CREATE INDEX claim_binding_sheet ON claim_binding(sheet_id, claim_id, id);
INSERT INTO claim_binding (sheet_id, claim_id, stated, stated_due, set_on)
    SELECT sheet_id, id, TRUE, stated_due, DATE '0001-01-01' FROM claim WHERE stated;
-- The history the as-of view reads, on top of that kept for a statement taken as of a date: every
-- change below is kept with the sheet's today when it was made (set_on / added_on / archived_on), so
-- the screen as it stood at the end of a date shows only the changes made while the sheet's today
-- was on or before it. What was already stored before this history was kept counts from the
-- beginning of time (0001-01-01, or null).

-- The sheet's today when it was archived (null: not archived, or from the beginning of time).
ALTER TABLE sheet ADD COLUMN archived_on DATE;

-- Every state a claim has been saved in, oldest first: the claim as it stood at the end of a date
-- is its last one kept on or before it. A claim with none on or before a date was not yet added.
CREATE TABLE claim_history (
    id BIGINT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
    sheet_id VARCHAR(200) NOT NULL REFERENCES sheet(id),
    claim_id BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES claim(id),
    person_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
    amount DECIMAL(19, 2) NOT NULL,
    claim_date DATE NOT NULL,
    note VARCHAR(1000) NOT NULL,
    status VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
    claim_number VARCHAR(200),
    settled_due DECIMAL(19, 2),
    opened_by VARCHAR(200),
    stated BOOLEAN NOT NULL,
    stated_due DECIMAL(19, 2),
    corrects VARCHAR(200),
    due_by DATE NOT NULL,
    deferred_until DATE,
    proofs INT NOT NULL,
    split_from VARCHAR(200),
    late_entry BOOLEAN NOT NULL,
    listed BIGINT,
    set_on DATE NOT NULL
);
CREATE INDEX claim_history_sheet ON claim_history(sheet_id, set_on, id);
INSERT INTO claim_history (sheet_id, claim_id, person_id, amount, claim_date, note, status, claim_number,
        settled_due, opened_by, stated, stated_due, corrects, due_by, deferred_until, proofs, split_from,
        late_entry, listed, set_on)
    SELECT sheet_id, id, person_id, amount, claim_date, note, status, claim_number, settled_due, opened_by,
        stated, stated_due, corrects, due_by, deferred_until, proofs, split_from, late_entry, listed,
        DATE '0001-01-01' FROM claim;

-- Every change to a person's statements, oldest first: their count, last due-total and date then.
CREATE TABLE person_statement_history (
    id BIGINT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
    sheet_id VARCHAR(200) NOT NULL REFERENCES sheet(id),
    person_id BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES person(id),
    statement_count INT NOT NULL,
    stated_total VARCHAR(30),
    statement_date DATE,
    set_on DATE NOT NULL

content.text:
Terms now count business days, and all 4 tests in the acceptance spec pass under `bin/e2e`.

**How the due-by is worked out now**
- I replaced `HolidayRepository.pastHolidays` with `dueBy(sheetId, date, terms)`. It counts forward from the day after the claim's date, skipping Saturdays, Sundays and the sheet's holidays, and stops on the terms-th business day it reaches. Terms of 0 gives the claim's date itself.
- All four places that set a due-by use it: adding a claim, pasting claims, splitting a claim, and the quick-add check for closed periods.
- Overdue, the late-charge boundaries and the period a claim belongs to all read the stored due-by, so they follow without further changes. The front end only displays what the server sends, so only its comments changed.
- A holiday added later still leaves an existing due-by as it is, because the due-by is fixed and stored when the claim is made.

**Claims already on the sheet**
- A new migration, `src/main/java/db/migration/V52__business_day_terms.java`, works out every stored due-by again, both on claims and in the claim history. It uses the holidays on the sheet at the time of the migration.
- The store doesn't keep the terms a claim was fixed with, so the migration recovers them from the old due-by: the days between the claim's date and its due-by, minus any holidays the due-by was pushed past.
- That recovery can't always be exact. If a stored due-by falls right after a run of holidays, the original terms could have pointed at any day in that run, and the migration assumes the first. This case is rare because holidays have only existed since the previous change. Saving the terms on each claim from now on would remove the guesswork; I didn't add that.
- The test database is in-memory and starts empty, so no test covers the migration. It ran cleanly at start-up, but has only ever run on an empty database.

I also updated the comments that described the old rule (date plus terms, moved past holidays) in the claim, holiday and overdue code.
